Chapter 9: The Wider World — Public Life, Justice, and the Habits of Hope
Let’s step outside the comfort of home, and away from the routines of work, for a minute. Think about how much the world around us shapes who we are—the news we hear, the neighborhoods we live in, and even the streets we walk every day. These places do more than fill our calendars; they quietly shape our hearts, often in ways we don’t even notice.
In a world that’s full of injustice, division, and fear, the habits we carry into public life matter more than ever.
Picture this: a few neighbors decide to clean up their local park. At first, it’s just about making the space look a bit nicer. But as they dig in—picking up litter, planting flowers—something starts to change. They get to know each other, share a few laughs, maybe even talk about their hopes for the neighborhood. That simple act of showing up and caring for a shared space starts to build a sense of hope and responsibility.
Or take another scene. In a different city, a congregation teams up with a local shelter to serve meals to folks who need them. Sometimes the work is messy and humbling. But as they keep coming back, this habit of serving starts to change everyone involved. It teaches us that every person matters, that justice isn’t just a big idea—it’s something you live out. And hope? It grows, little by little, through those small, faithful acts.
See, public life is packed with stories that compete for our attention—stories about scarcity, fear, and keeping to ourselves. It’s easy to get caught up in those, to turn cynical or just tune out. But the habits we practice out in the world have the power to shape our hearts for hope, for courage, and for justice.
This kind of transformation doesn’t just happen on its own. It takes intention—a real willingness to show up, to listen, and to act. The way we vote, the causes we back, and even how we treat strangers on the street—these are all habits that can shape our hearts for the common good.
Most people don’t realize how powerful these small acts can be. There’s a tendency to think that real change requires something huge, some kind of heroic effort. But over time, it’s the quiet, steady habits of justice and hope that make the difference. They form a heart that believes change is possible, a heart that won’t give in to despair, and one that finds real joy in working for the good of everyone.
The wider world is shaping us, every day. Its routines, its challenges, and its opportunities—all of these influence what we care about and who we become.
So, if we choose habits that aim our hearts toward justice, mercy, and hope, we’re not just forming ourselves—we’re helping shape a better world for everyone.
